newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU court rules against drug firms.
newsitem.headline: EU court rules against drug firms.

text.p: The European Union's pharmaceutical industry lost a key battle on Thursday in its campaign to block imports of cheap unpatented drugs from Spain and Portugal.

The European Court of Justice ruled that companies in other EU countries could not block such imports except under very limited circumstances, saying the principle of free movement of goods between EU countries must take precedence.

The case pitted Merck and Co Inc and SmithKline Beecham Plc against two British companies -- Primecrown Ltd and Europharm of Worthing Ltd -- who wanted to import drugs sold by drugs firms in Spain and Portugal, where government controls keep prices low.

Merck and Beecham tried to block the shipments on the grounds that the drugs -- Merck's Innovace, Proscar and Timoptol and Beecham's Augmentin -- were placed on the market at a time when Spain and Portugal did not offer patent protection.
They argued that it was unfair for products that were patented in Britain to face competition from unpatented drugs from countries with state price controls.

The decision should open the way for British importers to bring in about 30 drugs from Spain and Portugal, giving consumers more choice and helping to contain prices in Britain, John Barker, chairman of the Association of Pharmaceutical Importers, told Reuters.

European drugs companies began waging a multi-pronged campaign to try to block drugs from Spain and Portugal as a transition period in the 1985 treaty bringing those countries into the EU was set to expire.
The treaty allowed drugs patentholders to block imports from the two newcomers until three years after they had made the products patentable -- a period the court ruled had now ended.
The court said companies could not bar shipments of products that they had willingly put on the market, citing EU treaty rules requiring countries to remove internal trade barriers.

"There can be no doubt...that if a patentee could prohibit the importation of protected products marketed in another member state by him or with his consent, he would be able to partition national markets and thereby restrict trade between the member states," it said.
The court said companies could restrict imports only when they had been legally required to market the products in the exporting country -- which did not apply in this case.

Pharmaceutical companies lost a campaign last year to get the European Commission to allow seven EU countries to invoke a "safeguard" clause in Spain's membership treaty so they could continue blocking pharmaceutical imports.
The Commission said it was not convinced the exports would cause the pharmaceutical industries in those countries serious and persistent difficulties as required by the clause.
Unusually, the Court of Justice rejected the advice of one of its advocates-general, who issued an opinion in June supporting Merck and Beecham.
Merck and the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries' Associatios said they would issue statements on the case later in the day. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
